title: Fig Jam
subtitle: Fresh-fig conserve with lemon, sweet, jammy, and full of seeds
excerpt: Fresh fig jam is rich and honey-sweet with a distinctive seedy texture from the fruit's interior. Lemon juice brightens it and helps the set. Best made in late summer when figs are at their ripest. Makes about three 450 g jars.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (PG #10136); Pam Corbin, Preserves. Figs are low in pectin and need lemon juice or added pectin for a reliable set.

recipe.batchNotes: Up to 1.5 kg figs works cleanly.

content.text: Fresh fig jam has a jammy, honeyed sweetness quite different from any berry preserve. The seeds from inside the fruit give it a distinctive texture, and the flavour concentrates beautifully during cooking. Lemon juice is essential,  without it, fig jam often stays too soft to hold a proper set. Makes about three 450 g jars.

items.prepNote: very ripe, stalks removed, roughly chopped
zest only (pare with a peeler, no white pith)

content.text: Mix the chopped figs, sugar, lemon juice, and zest (if using) in the jam pan. Cover and leave for 2 hours or overnight. The figs release juice and the sugar begins to dissolve.

Set the pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar is fully dissolved. Raise to a rolling boil and cook for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. Fig jam can catch on the base of the pan,  keep moving it. Test on a cold plate from 15 minutes. When the surface wrinkles, remove from the heat, skim, rest 5 minutes, then ladle into hot sterilised jars and seal.

items.cause: High sugar concentration in fig jam clings to the pan base.
items.fix: Stir more frequently, especially in the last 5 minutes. A heavy-based pan helps significantly.

items.cause: Very ripe figs have high natural sugar.
items.fix: Reduce sugar to 650 g per kg fruit and add an extra tablespoon of lemon juice.
Return to the pan, add 2 tbsp more lemon juice and 1 tsp pectin, boil another 5 minutes and test again.

items.cause: Figs not chopped small enough before cooking.
items.fix: Mash with a potato masher mid-cook, or use a stick blender briefly at the end before jarring.
